_about: Reviewed safety facts shown on profile pages (Q4 plan E2/E3; gaps in docs/research/is-x-safe-question-audit-2026-10-06.md). Every fact names its public source and its evidence class: 'observed' (we checked it ourselves on the date given), 'declared' (the publisher's own statement, not verified by us) or 'source' (read from the project's code or repository). Facts never change scores or ranks. Add a fact only with a source; remove it when the source changes or disappears. Topics: operator, access, data, security.

facts.text: Run by Sampark Inc, doing business as Composio. Its terms are governed by Delaware law.
An agent using Composio can act in every app you connect, within the scopes you granted. Composio's own advice is to treat those scopes like production credentials.
Composio's cloud stores the OAuth access and refresh tokens and API keys of the apps you connect, and uses them to call those apps on your behalf. Using your own OAuth app doesn't change that.
Those credentials are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM) with keys Composio holds by default. Customer-managed keys, a private VPC or self-hosting are enterprise arrangements.
Connected-account tokens are redacted from API responses by default, and a Zero Data Retention option stops call payloads from being stored.
States SOC 2 Type II compliance. The report and the sub-processor list are in its trust center, trust.composio.dev. Vulnerability reports go to security@composio.dev.
GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled on the repository, which has a SECURITY.md. composio.dev serves no security.txt.
Made by Cline Bot Inc.
Runs in your editor or terminal and can read and edit files, run terminal commands, use a browser and call MCP servers. Each kind of action has its own auto-approve setting.
In the VS Code extension, reading and editing files, using the browser and calling MCP servers are auto-approved by default; terminal commands ask first.
Works with the model provider you choose (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter and others), or with a local model through Ollama or LM Studio.
Cline's own telemetry excludes code, file contents and paths, command arguments, conversation content and API keys, and can be turned off in settings.
cline.bot publishes a security.txt (security@cline.bot), the repository has a SECURITY.md, and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.
Its maintainers have published 3 security advisories (1 critical, 1 high, 1 low), all in the last 12 months.
Run by SideGuide Technologies, Inc., doing business as Firecrawl, a Delaware corporation.
You can run Firecrawl on your own servers instead of using its hosted API.
States SOC 2 Type 2. Vulnerability reports go to a Bugcrowd program with safe harbor.
firecrawl.dev publishes a security.txt. The repository has no SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.
Its maintainers have published 4 security advisories (1 critical, 3 high), 2 of them in the last 12 months.
Run by LangGenius, Inc., a Delaware corporation.
States SOC 2 Type II (audited by Sensiba), ISO 27001:2022 (Johanson) and GDPR compliance, as of March 2026.
Its maintainers have published 21 security advisories (8 high, 10 medium, 3 low), 14 of them in the last 12 months.
The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled. dify.ai serves no security.txt.
Each sandbox runs in its own Firecracker microVM with its own kernel, so code is isolated at the hypervisor boundary rather than in a container.
Sandboxes are destroyed on timeout or shutdown. A paused sandbox keeps its filesystem and memory until it is resumed.

Holds a SOC 2 Type II report, available under NDA from trust.e2b.dev, and signs HIPAA BAAs on Enterprise plans. Vulnerability reports go to security@e2b.dev; testing against E2B needs prior written consent.
GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled on the SDK repository, which has no SECURITY.md. e2b.dev serves no security.txt.
Made by Anthropic. The repository's licence reserves all rights and puts use under Anthropic's Commercial Terms, so it isn't open source.
Interactive sessions start in Auto mode, where a classifier model approves or blocks actions. In Manual mode it starts read-only and asks before editing files or running commands.
Its file tools ask before reading or writing outside the folder it started in, but a shell command you approve can write anywhere your user account can unless you turn on its sandbox.

Prompts and model output go to Anthropic, or to Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry if you configure one. Commercial accounts: kept 30 days and not used for training. Consumer accounts: used for training when that setting is on (kept 5 years), otherwise kept 30 days.

Session transcripts are stored on your machine in plain text under ~/.claude/projects/ for 30 days by default. Usage metrics exclude code, prompts and file paths and can be turned off with DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1.
Anthropic publishes its SOC 2 Type 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate in its trust center, trust.anthropic.com. Vulnerabilities go to a HackerOne program.
Its maintainers have published 33 security advisories (26 high, 4 medium, 3 low), 23 of them in the last 12 months. The repository has a SECURITY.md.
Made by OpenAI. The CLI is open source under Apache-2.0.

In a version-controlled folder it recommends its Auto preset, which reads, edits and runs commands in the working directory without asking. Writes stay in that workspace, and network access is off unless you enable it.
Those limits are enforced by the operating system: Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap with seccomp on Linux, and a WSL2 or native sandbox on Windows.
openai.com's security.txt points to a Bugcrowd program, and the repository has a SECURITY.md.
Its maintainers have published 1 security advisory (high), in September 2025.
The Agents framework is open source under Apache-2.0. Agents connect to LiveKit Cloud, the company's hosted service, or to a self-hosted LiveKit server.
LiveKit Cloud doesn't keep media or transcripts by default: recordings are written to your own S3, GCS or Azure bucket, and prompts, audio and completions for AI inference aren't logged.
States SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and CCPA compliance and EU–US Data Privacy Framework certification, and signs HIPAA BAAs on Scale and Enterprise plans. Reports are in its trust center, trust.livekit.io.

livekit.io publishes a security.txt (security@livekit.io), and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled on the repository. Its maintainers have published 1 security advisory (medium), in the last 12 months.
Run by Freebuff, Inc., which also operates Codebuff.
It collects prompts, code, files and repository data, which are processed by its own systems and by AI model providers.
It shows ads: prompts and messages may be analysed to select and measure them, including by deriving general interest categories.
It doesn't train models on your prompts or project data unless it says so before you use that model or feature.
freebuff.com's security.txt lists support@codebuff.com. The repository has a SECURITY.md; GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.
Run by Anaconda, Inc. with its affiliate Kilo Code Inc.
Paid plans can switch off retention of AI prompts and outputs, with controls over which model providers requests are routed to.
SOC 2 documentation is available in its trust center, trust.kilo.ai. The page doesn't say which report type.
kilo.ai publishes a security.txt (security@kilo.ai), and the repository has a SECURITY.md.
Its API listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default, so only your own machine can reach it. Setting OLLAMA_HOST, for example to 0.0.0.0, opens it to your network.

Local models run on your machine and Ollama doesn't see the prompts. With cloud-hosted models it processes prompts and responses, and says it doesn't store or log that content or train on it. Cloud features can be switched off for local-only use.

OSV lists 31 advisories for the github.com/ollama/ollama Go module, the most recent published in July 2026. Ollama publishes no GitHub security advisories; reports go through its SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting.
Made by Mintplex Labs Inc.
Sends anonymous usage telemetry unless you turn it off, in Settings > Privacy or with DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true. With telemetry off it still contacts its CDN to download models.

Its maintainers have published 25 security advisories (1 critical, 7 high, 11 medium, 6 low), 23 of them in the last 12 months. The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.

Most tool permissions default to "allow", meaning they run without approval. The exceptions: it asks before reaching paths outside the project, and blocks reading .env files. Setting bash and edit to "ask" in opencode.json adds approvals.
Its maintainers have published 3 security advisories (1 critical, 2 high), all in the last 12 months. The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.
It lets the AI client you connect read and write files and run any terminal command on your machine; the project calls it a privileged local automation tool.

Its allowed-directories setting and command blocklist are guardrails against accidents, not a security boundary: terminal commands can still reach files outside the allowed directories. For real isolation the project recommends Docker or a virtual machine.
It doesn't try to tell a genuine request from prompt injection; it assumes the connected AI client is trusted.
Telemetry is on by default and can be turned off. It records base command names without their arguments, and no names, email addresses or file paths.
Tool calls and their arguments are also logged locally on the machine running it; those logs aren't uploaded.
OSV lists 2 advisories for its npm package, @wonderwhy-er/desktop-commander, published in June 2026. The repository has a SECURITY.md; GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.

Tools, Functions, Pipes and Filters run arbitrary Python code on the server. Its docs say only trusted administrators should be able to install them, and that a listing on the community site isn't a security review.
Its Open Terminal add-on gives agents a terminal and a filesystem.
Vulnerability reports are accepted only through GitHub's private reporting.
Its maintainers have published 165 security advisories (1 critical, 71 high, 86 medium, 7 low), 162 of them in the last 12 months. openwebui.com publishes a security.txt.
Chat history, settings and API keys are stored on your device, with no cloud sync. Prompts go directly to the model provider you configure, not through Cherry Studio's servers.
It collects aggregated feature usage and anonymised crash logs, which you can switch off under Settings > Data Settings > Privacy Settings. It says it never collects API keys or conversations.
Its maintainers have published 4 security advisories, all rated critical, 1 of them in the last 12 months. The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.
Its execute_blender_code tool runs arbitrary Python inside Blender. The README warns to use it with caution and always save your work first.
The Blender add-on runs a socket server that listens on localhost by default.

Sends a minimal anonymous usage record by default (tool name, success, timing, versions, operating system). Prompts, generated code and screenshots are collected only if you opt in, and DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true turns telemetry off entirely.
The repository has no SECURITY.md, and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.
Runs locally as a proxy between your agent and the model provider, so prompts, tool outputs, logs and files pass through it.

An anonymous telemetry beacon is on by default. It reports compression ratios, counters, provider and model IDs, operating system and architecture, and never prompts, completions, code or file paths. HEADROOM_BEACON=off, DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or --offline turns it off.
Its maintainers have published 1 security advisory (high), in the last 12 months. The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.
Its README, which is in Chinese, says it works by having your agent run shell commands, such as pip install, mcporter and twitter.
Cookies and tokens for logged-in platforms stay on your machine, in ~/.agent-reach/config.yaml with owner-only (600) permissions, and aren't uploaded.
The README warns that scripting platforms such as Twitter or Xiaohongshu with your cookies risks an account ban, and recommends a dedicated secondary account.
The repository has a SECURITY.md; GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.
Made by NVIDIA; open source under Apache-2.0.
Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox: kernel controls confine which files and system calls it can use, and every network connection passes through a policy.
Sends anonymous telemetry limited to operational categories and counts, not sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials or user content. OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false turns it off.
The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.
Gives an assistant access to public CKAN open-data portals: search datasets, explore organisations, query tabular data and read metadata.
You can run it on your own machine or use the project's hosted endpoint, which has a shared request quota.

Its maintainers have published 15 security advisories (1 critical, 2 high, 10 medium, 2 low), all in the last 12 months. The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.

Starts in Auto mode by default: a classifier model approves safe file edits and shell commands and blocks risky ones. Ask Permissions mode asks before every edit and command; YOLO approves everything.
Its Chrome extension acts inside your Chrome profile, including signed-in pages, and browser results may be sent to the configured AI provider.
Prompts and code go to the provider you sign in with (Qwen, Alibaba Cloud, or your own API key's provider), and that provider's privacy terms apply.
The repository has a SECURITY.md; GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.
A self-hosted workspace whose agents can use local or API models, tools, MCP, files and a shell.
Its README advises keeping authentication on, setting LOCALHOST_BYPASS=false outside local development, and not exposing raw model or service ports publicly.
The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.

An ops agent for your infrastructure. Its features include remote execution and a reverse-tunnel browser SSH shell into any host, alongside read-only inspection tools in a bash sandbox; it says every call is audited.
The repository has a SECURITY.md and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled.
Commits each edit it makes to git with a descriptive message, so /undo can discard the last change. --no-auto-commits turns that off.
Connects to almost any LLM, including local models; prompts and code go to the one you configure.
Analytics are collected only if you opt in, and never include your code, chat messages or keys.
The repository has no SECURITY.md, and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is off.
